scenario_stem:
Ironvale Fasteners Co is a private limited company employing 96 workers at its steel bolt and nut factory in Country X. Output reached 1.8 million units last year, up 12% on the previous 12 months. Priya Nair, the operations manager, reports that 34% of bolts failed quality checks in March, and two line supervisors resigned after a dispute over overtime. Workers are paid a time rate of $9.50 per hour and work 44 hours per week.

Priya is considering two ways to improve motivation on the shop floor. Option A: switch the 60 line workers to a piece rate of $0.09 per approved bolt, based on Taylor's scientific management. Option B: keep the time rate and invest $18,000 in a recognition scheme, giving monthly certificates and a $150 bonus for the team with the lowest defect rate, linked to Herzberg's theory. She must decide before the new contract is signed in 6 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'Maslow's hierarchy of needs'.
questions.model_answer: Maslow's hierarchy of needs is a theory that arranges human needs in five levels — physiological, safety, social, esteem and self-actualisation — where lower-level needs must be met before higher-level needs can motivate employees [2].

knowledge_max_2: Needs are arranged in a hierarchy or levels (physiological to self-actualisation)
Lower-level needs must be satisfied before higher-level needs motivate

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why a well-motivated workforce is important to Ironvale Fasteners Co.
questions.model_answer: A well-motivated workforce matters because motivated workers produce more output per hour, raising productivity so Ironvale can grow beyond 1.8 million units with the same 96 workers [k]. Higher productivity spreads fixed costs over more bolts, lowering the average cost per unit and protecting the margin needed to fund the $18,000 scheme [app]. Second, motivated workers take greater care and make fewer mistakes [k]. Fewer errors mean the 34% defect rate seen in March should fall, so fewer bolts are scrapped and Ironvale's reputation with its new contract customer is protected [app].

knowledge_max_2: Motivated workers are more productive / higher output per worker
Motivated workers make fewer errors / take greater care
application_max_2: Reference to 1.8 million units output / 96 workers
Reference to 34% defect rate in March / scrap and reputation

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Ironvale Fasteners Co might face if it introduces the piece rate (Option A).
questions.model_answer: First, a problem is that piece rate can reduce quality [k]. Paying $0.09 per approved bolt pushes workers to produce bolts as fast as possible, so defect rates could climb above the 34% recorded in March [app], and higher defects would damage Ironvale's standing with clients, leading to lost orders and rework costs [an]. Second, piece rate rewards individual speed, not teamwork [k]. Taylor's scientific management treats each worker separately, so experienced staff may refuse to help the slower of the 60 line workers [app], and the friction could trigger more disputes like the one that cost the factory two supervisors, raising labour turnover [an].

knowledge_max_2: Piece rate can push workers to rush / quality may fall
Piece rate rewards individual effort / weakens teamwork
application_max_2: Reference to $0.09 per approved bolt / 34% defect rate in March
Reference to Taylor's scientific management / 60 line workers / two supervisors resigned
analysis_max_2: Chain from rushing to more defects to lost orders / rework costs
Chain from individual reward to friction to disputes / higher labour turnover

questions.question_text: Do you think Ironvale Fasteners Co should switch to the piece rate (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A follows Taylor's scientific management: paying $0.09 per approved bolt links pay directly to output, so the 60 line workers would be driven to maximise production and Ironvale could lift output above 1.8 million units [k]. Because only approved bolts are paid, workers also carry the quality risk themselves, creating a direct incentive to avoid the defects that reached 34% in March [app]. Higher throughput would spread fixed costs over more units, improving efficiency and competitiveness [an]. However, Option B targets Herzberg's theory and Maslow's esteem needs [k]. Monthly certificates and a $150 team bonus reward the whole team for the lowest defect rate while keeping the $9.50 per hour base pay unchanged, so the $18,000 cost is predictable [app]. This addresses the overtime dispute and low morale directly, whereas piece rate could inflame them further [an]. Overall, I think Option B is the better choice [eval] because Ironvale's central problem is quality — a 34% failure rate — and Herzberg shows pay alone does not remove dissatisfaction; recognition and team effort do [eval].

Herzberg: motivators (recognition) / hygiene factors (pay) distinction

Reference to Option B: $18,000 scheme / $150 team bonus / $9.50 per hour

Chain from recognition scheme to morale / quality improvement vs overtime dispute

scenario_stem:
Copperfield Electronics Assembly is a public limited company that builds circuit boards for home appliances in Country X. The factory employs 210 production-line workers and 18 quality inspectors. Annual revenue reached $26 million last year, but average labour turnover on the assembly line hit 22%, with 58 workers leaving in 12 months. Pay is a salary of $1,450 per month and staff describe the work as repetitive.

Managing Director Elena Brooks is choosing between two motivation strategies. Option A: apply Taylor's scientific management more strictly — time-and-motion studies, a 10-week training programme for new hires, and a piece rate of $2.10 per tested board. Option B: introduce job rotation between three assembly stations every 4 hours, plus a $90 monthly attendance bonus. Elena must present her recommendation to the board in 10 days.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'Taylor's scientific management'.
questions.model_answer: Taylor's scientific management is the theory that workers are motivated principally by money, using time-and-motion studies to find the one best way to do each job and paying a piece rate linked to how much each worker produces [2].

knowledge_max_2: Workers motivated mainly / principally by money
Time-and-motion studies identify the one best way / pay linked to output via piece rate

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why labour turnover on the assembly line is high at Copperfield Electronics Assembly.
questions.model_answer: One reason is that the work is repetitive, so workers become bored and see no challenge in the job [k]. Repeating the same assembly stations all day adds no variety or new skills, removing Herzberg's motivators such as responsibility, so the 210 production-line workers drift towards quitting — 58 left in the last 12 months [app]. A second reason is that pay does not reward effort [k]. A salary of $1,450 per month is paid regardless of output, so productive and unproductive workers earn the same, and turnover has hit 22% [app].

knowledge_max_2: Repetitive work causes boredom / removes Herzberg's motivators
Salary is fixed regardless of output, so effort is not rewarded
application_max_2: Reference to 58 workers leaving in 12 months / 210 production-line workers
Reference to $1,450 per month salary / 22% turnover

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Copperfield Electronics Assembly of introducing Option B (job rotation).
questions.model_answer: One benefit is reduced boredom [k]. Moving each worker between three assembly stations every 4 hours adds variety and fresh skills to a repetitive job [app], and less boredom means fewer errors and fewer absences, helping the 210 production-line workers sustain daily output [an]. A second benefit is greater flexibility [k]. With every worker trained on three stations, cover is available whenever colleagues are absent, so the 18 quality inspectors receive a steadier flow of comparable boards [app], reducing bottlenecks and protecting the $26 million annual revenue [an].

knowledge_max_2: Job rotation adds variety / reduces boredom
Job rotation makes workers multi-skilled / flexible cover
application_max_2: Reference to three assembly stations every 4 hours / repetitive work
Reference to 210 production-line workers / 18 quality inspectors / $26 million revenue
analysis_max_2: Chain from variety to lower boredom to fewer errors / absences / sustained output
Chain from multi-skilling to flex cover to steady flow / protected revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think Copperfield Electronics Assembly should introduce Option A? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A is built on Taylor's theory that money drives effort: a piece rate of $2.10 per tested board would reward fast workers, so tested output per worker should rise above current levels [k]. Time-and-motion studies and a 10-week training programme would also standardise methods for new hires, helping stabilise a workforce that lost 58 workers in 12 months [app]. Higher tested output spreads overheads over more boards, improving cost efficiency [an]. However, Option B tackles why people are leaving — repetitive, unchallenging work [k]. Job rotation between three assembly stations every 4 hours adds variety, and the $90 monthly attendance bonus rewards presence without raising the $1,450 basic salary bill unpredictably [app]. Retention of skilled assemblers also protects quality, which the 18 inspectors police on every board before it reaches home-appliance clients [an]. Overall, I think Option B is the stronger choice [eval] because 58 workers left in 12 months mainly from monotony, and Herzberg's theory shows adding variety keeps people better than paying more for the same dull job [eval].

Herzberg: hygiene factors vs motivators / variety reduces dissatisfaction

Reference to Option B: three assembly stations every 4 hours / $90 monthly attendance bonus / $1,450 salary

scenario_stem:
Halcyon Ceramics Ltd employs 78 workers at its pottery factory near Country X's capital city. The factory produces 3,400 hand-decorated plates per month. Workers are paid $11.20 per hour and eat in a cramped canteen with no heating. Absenteeism reached 9% last winter and 11 workers resigned in the last 6 months. The production director, Marcus Vale, wants to raise morale before a large export order.

Marcus is weighing two investments. Option A: spend $40,000 improving hygiene factors — a heated canteen, better lockers and a quiet rest room — reflecting Herzberg's view that conditions must be adequate before motivators can work. Option B: spend the same $40,000 on motivators — job enrichment, monthly recognition boards and team leaders with responsibility for quality on each kiln line. He must decide this month.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'Herzberg's two-factor theory'.
questions.model_answer: Herzberg's two-factor theory states that job satisfaction and dissatisfaction come from different factors: hygiene factors such as pay and conditions prevent dissatisfaction, while motivators such as recognition, responsibility and advancement create satisfaction and encourage effort [2].

knowledge_max_2: Job satisfaction and dissatisfaction arise from different factors
Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction; motivators create satisfaction

questions.question_text: Explain two hygiene factors Halcyon Ceramics Ltd should improve.
questions.model_answer: One hygiene factor is working conditions [k]. The canteen has no heating and lockers are poor, so making these comfortable would remove a daily irritation, helping to cut the 9% absenteeism recorded last winter [app]. A second hygiene factor is rest and recovery space [k]. A quiet rest room for the 78 workers would ease fatigue during long kiln shifts, so people return to work on the 3,400 hand-decorated plates with more care rather than after a miserable break [app].

knowledge_max_2: Working conditions are a hygiene factor
Rest or facilities are hygiene factors that prevent dissatisfaction
application_max_2: Reference to cramped canteen with no heating / lockers
Reference to 9% absenteeism / 78 workers / 3,400 plates

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Halcyon Ceramics Ltd of spending the $40,000 on motivators (Option B).
questions.model_answer: One benefit is greater responsibility and esteem [k]. Giving team leaders responsibility for quality on each kiln line meets Maslow's esteem level and gives workers a real voice in standards [app], so workers take ownership of each batch and defect rates on the 3,400 plates should fall [an]. A second benefit is recognition of good performance [k]. Monthly recognition boards make strong performance visible and job enrichment adds variety to decorating work [app], and motivated workers are more productive and less likely to join the 11 who resigned in the last 6 months [an].

knowledge_max_2: Responsibility and esteem are motivators / create satisfaction
Recognition and job enrichment are motivators
application_max_2: Reference to team leaders on each kiln line / responsibility for quality
Reference to monthly recognition boards / job enrichment / 11 workers resigned
analysis_max_2: Chain from responsibility to ownership to lower defect rates
Chain from recognition to motivation to higher productivity / lower turnover

questions.question_text: Do you think Halcyon Ceramics Ltd should choose Option A? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A is strongly supported by Herzberg: hygiene factors like a heated canteen and better lockers do not motivate on their own, but when they are poor they create dissatisfaction that blocks everything else [k]. The $40,000 would immediately improve daily life for all 78 workers, directly tackling the discomfort behind last winter's 9% absenteeism and the 11 resignations in 6 months [app]. Fixing dissatisfaction first stabilises the team before a demanding export order [an]. However, Option B adds only true motivators — job enrichment, recognition boards and team-leader responsibility — which Herzberg argues create genuine satisfaction and extra effort [k]. The pay of $11.20 per hour is presumably adequate, so further comfort may simply become the new normal, whereas motivators keep adding satisfaction [app]. Motivators build long-term engagement and quality ownership across the export order's production run [an]. Overall, I think Halcyon should choose Option A first [eval] because Herzberg is explicit that hygiene factors must be adequate before motivators can work — you cannot enrich jobs for workers shivering in an unheated canteen [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Herzberg: hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction / are prerequisites
Herzberg: motivators create satisfaction / extra effort
application_max_2: Reference to Option A: heated canteen / lockers / rest room / $40,000
Reference to Option B: job enrichment / recognition boards / $11.20 per hour

Chain from motivators to long-term engagement / quality ownership

scenario_stem:
Merryfield Confectionery is a private limited company making chocolate truffles in Country X. It employs 64 production-line workers across 2 shifts and 9 packaging staff. Sales reached $4.2 million last year, with 5 quality assurance inspectors checking every batch. Line workers report feeling 'stuck' with no chance of promotion, and 17 resigned in the past year. Pay is $10.60 per hour on both shifts.

The owner, Dana Whitmore, is considering either Option A: promote 2 experienced line workers to team-leader posts at $13.80 per hour, creating advancement on Herzberg's list of motivators, or Option B: keep everyone on $10.60 and introduce a profit-sharing scheme paying 4% of annual profit into a staff bonus fund shared equally. She needs to decide before the autumn rush.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'motivators'.
questions.model_answer: Motivators, in Herzberg's two-factor theory, are factors such as recognition, responsibility, advancement and the work itself that create job satisfaction and encourage employees to work harder and better [2].

knowledge_max_2: Motivators create job satisfaction (not just prevent dissatisfaction)
Examples: recognition / responsibility / advancement / the work itself

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Merryfield Confectionery's line workers feel 'stuck'.
questions.model_answer: One reason is the near absence of promotion opportunities [k]. With only 9 packaging staff and 5 quality assurance inspectors above the line, there are few senior roles to aim for, so ambition stalls on the production floor [app]. A second reason is a lack of responsibility and recognition [k]. Workers make truffles with no say in quality decisions and no advancement path, so Herzberg's motivators are missing — which helps explain why 17 resigned in the past year [app].

knowledge_max_2: Few promotion opportunities / career progression available
Lack of responsibility or recognition (Herzberg's motivators missing)
application_max_2: Reference to 9 packaging staff and 5 QA inspectors above the line / no chance of promotion
Reference to 17 resigned in the past year / feeling 'stuck'

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Merryfield Confectionery of Option A (promoting 2 line workers to team-leader posts).
questions.model_answer: One benefit is a visible signal that effort is rewarded [k]. Promoting 2 experienced line workers to team-leader posts at $13.80 per hour shows 64 colleagues that loyalty can lead to advancement [app], and the post costs only $3.20 per hour more while strongly lifting esteem and retention on the line [an]. A second benefit is better on-the-job leadership [k]. Team leaders drawn from the line know the truffle process intimately and can take responsibility for shift quality [app], reducing the load on the 5 quality assurance inspectors and protecting the $4.2 million sales revenue [an].

knowledge_max_2: Promotion signals effort is rewarded / advancement is a Herzberg motivator
Team leaders provide leadership / responsibility on the line
application_max_2: Reference to 2 experienced line workers to team-leader posts at $13.80 per hour / 64 colleagues
Reference to 5 quality assurance inspectors / $4.2 million sales
analysis_max_2: Chain from visible advancement to esteem to better retention

questions.question_text: Do you think Merryfield Confectionery should choose Option A? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A applies Herzberg's advancement motivator and Maslow's esteem needs [k]. Promoting 2 experienced line workers to team-leader posts at $13.80 per hour shows the whole line that effort leads somewhere, so staff should commit more strongly before the autumn rush [app]. Giving leaders authority over shift quality also builds skills in-house and eases supervision pressure on Dana Whitmore [an]. However, Option B shares financial success with everyone [k]. Keeping everyone on $10.60 avoids internal pay friction, and the 4% of annual profit is split equally, so even packaging staff participate in the reward [app]. But profit depends on factors beyond worker effort, such as cocoa and sugar costs, so the 4% fund may be small per person and weakly linked to individual performance [an]. Overall, I think Option A is the better first step [eval] because advancement and responsibility are true motivators that directly answer why 17 resigned, while an equal profit share would be felt only weakly on the line [eval].

Profit-sharing rewards company-wide success, not individual effort

scenario_stem:
Northgate Textiles is a private limited company weaving denim fabric in Country X. The mill employs 130 weavers across 3 production lines and pays a time rate of $8.90 per hour. Last year the mill produced 2.6 million metres of denim, but customer rejections reached 7.5% of orders. Managing Director Sofia Grant believes workers put in little discretionary effort because pay is not linked to results.

Sofia is considering Option A: replace the time rate with a piece rate of $0.07 per accepted metre across all 3 lines, following Taylor's scientific management. Option B: keep $8.90 per hour and introduce a team bonus of $220 per month for each line that keeps rejections below 5%. The board meets in 2 weeks to decide.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'bonus'.
questions.model_answer: A bonus is an additional financial reward paid on top of normal wages or salary when an employee or team reaches a set target, such as an output level, quality standard or sales figure [2].

knowledge_max_2: Extra / additional financial reward on top of normal pay
Paid for reaching a target (output / quality / sales)

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Northgate Textiles should not rely on the time rate alone.
questions.model_answer: One reason is that time rate pays for hours, not results [k]. At $8.90 per hour, fast weavers earn the same as slow ones, so there is little incentive to push beyond the 2.6 million metres produced last year [app]. A second reason is that time rate ignores quality [k]. Workers are paid the same however many metres are rejected, so nothing in the pay system discourages the 7.5% rejection rate that is costing orders [app].

knowledge_max_2: Time rate pays for hours not results / low incentive to work harder
Time rate ignores quality / does not discourage waste
application_max_2: Reference to $8.90 per hour / 2.6 million metres
Reference to 7.5% rejection rate / costing orders

questions.question_text: Explain two possible problems with Option A (a piece rate of $0.07 per accepted metre).
questions.model_answer: One problem is quality risk [k]. Paying $0.07 per accepted metre pushes weavers to rush, and disputes over what counts as 'accepted' could rise, so rejections could climb above 7.5% [app], damaging Northgate's reputation with denim buyers and inviting more rejected orders [an]. A second problem is unstable incomes [k]. Piece rate pay swings with machine stoppages and order books, so the 130 weavers could take home very different amounts each week [app], which may demotivate cautious workers and increase labour turnover at the mill [an].

Piece rate incomes vary week to week / unstable

Reference to 130 weavers / machine stoppages / order books

Chain from income instability to demotivation to higher turnover

questions.question_text: Do you think Northgate Textiles should switch to the piece rate (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A follows Taylor's scientific management by linking pay to output [k]. At $0.07 per accepted metre, fast weavers earn more, so output should rise above 2.6 million metres a year, and because rejected metres are unpaid, workers also shoulder part of the quality risk behind the 7.5% rejection rate [app]. Higher throughput would spread fixed costs over more metres, cutting unit cost [an]. Option B, by contrast, keeps the $8.90 per hour base and adds a $220 monthly team bonus per line for holding rejections below 5% [k]. This targets Northgate's real emergency — 7.5% rejections — with a shared team goal, and earnings do not swing with machine stoppages, keeping the 130 weavers financially secure [app]. A team bonus also builds cooperation on the line, which Taylor's individual piece rate undermines [an]. Overall, I think Option B is the better choice [eval] because the urgent problem is a 7.5% rejection rate, and the $220 team bonus attacks that directly while keeping pay stable for the 130 weavers [eval].

Team bonus builds cooperation / shared goal vs individual competition

scenario_stem:
Redstone Aluminium Die-Casting is a private limited company producing brake housings for motorbikes in Country X. The plant cast 240,000 brake housings last year. It employs 84 machine operators and 12 health-and-safety inspectors across 2 shifts. Last year 27 accidents were reported, more than double the 13 recorded 2 years ago. Workers mention stress, noise at 95 decibels and fear of burns from molten metal. Pay is $12.40 per hour.

Managing Director Viktor Lam must choose between two options. Option A: invest $55,000 in extra safety — extraction fans, heat shields and quieter machines — targeting Maslow's safety needs. Option B: raise all 96 workers' pay by 8% to $13.39 per hour, arguing that a stronger financial reward will lift morale. A safety audit is due in 8 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'motivation'.
questions.model_answer: Motivation is the factors inside and around a job that encourage employees to behave in ways that achieve business objectives, such as working hard, taking care over quality and staying with the employer [2].

knowledge_max_2: Motivation is the drive / factors that encourage employees to work well
Motivated employees work hard / take care / stay with the employer

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Redstone Aluminium Die-Casting should invest in safety before raising pay.
questions.model_answer: One reason is Maslow's hierarchy of needs [k]. With 27 accidents last year, noise at 95 decibels and fear of burns from molten metal, workers cannot move up the hierarchy towards esteem and self-actualisation while they feel physically unsafe [app]. A second reason is that accidents destroy productivity and cost money [k]. Every injury means lost shifts and investigation time across the 2 shifts, so preventing injuries is cheaper and more reliable than enduring them [app].

knowledge_max_2: Maslow: safety needs must be met before higher needs motivate
Accidents cost money / lost time / investigations
application_max_2: Reference to 27 accidents / 95 decibels / fear of burns from molten metal

questions.model_answer: One benefit is fewer accidents [k]. Extraction fans, heat shields and quieter machines would cut exposure to fumes, burns and noise, so the 27 accidents reported last year should fall towards the 13 seen 2 years ago [app], keeping the 84 machine operators productive and the 2 shifts running on schedule [an]. A second benefit is a stronger audit outcome [k]. The improvements directly answer the safety audit due in 8 weeks and show the workforce that management takes its duties seriously [app], which should lift confidence, morale and willingness to stay at the plant [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Redstone Aluminium Die-Casting should choose Option A? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A targets the real problem: fear [k]. Maslow's hierarchy shows safety needs must be met before higher motivation is possible, and with 27 accidents more than double the 13 recorded 2 years ago, plus 95 decibel noise, no pay rise makes molten metal safer [app]. The $55,000 covers physical safeguards used by all 96 workers, and passing the 8-week safety audit protects production of the 240,000 brake housings a year [an]. Option B is simpler — 8% more pay, $13.39 per hour for every worker, no machinery changes [k]. Herzberg would class this as a hygiene factor: welcome, but it prevents dissatisfaction rather than creating motivation, so the fear of burns persists [app]. scenario_stem:
Clearway Glassworks is a private limited company making laboratory glass tubing in Country X. It employs 52 glass-blowers and 14 packers. Output averages 9,500 metres of tubing per month at a defect rate of 4%. Pay is a salary of $1,380 per month for blowers. The owner, Helena Ortiz, notes that quit rates among young blowers reach 15% a year and blames low pay.

Helena is considering two reward options for the blowers. Option A: a profit-sharing scheme paying 3% of annual profit, about $70,000 this year, split equally among all 66 staff. Option B: an individual bonus of $60 per month for each blower whose defect rate stays under 2%, payable for up to 5 months per year. She wants a decision at the June review.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'teamworking'.
questions.model_answer: Teamworking is organising employees into groups that share responsibility for a task or goal, pooling skills, supporting one another and taking collective ownership of the result [2].

knowledge_max_2: Employees organised into groups sharing responsibility for a task/goal
Pool skills / support one another / collective ownership

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Clearway Glassworks could use Maslow's hierarchy of needs to motivate its glass-blowers.
questions.model_answer: One way is to meet safety needs [k]. Glass-blowing involves molten glass, so better heat-resistant gloves and face protection would reduce the 15% annual quit rate among young blowers by making the workshop feel safe [app]. A second way is to meet esteem needs [k]. Recognising blowers whose defect rate is under 2% with a certificate would make them feel respected and valued, matching the pride Herzberg says esteem-level recognition creates [app].

Esteem needs: recognition / respect / achievement

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks of Option B (an individual bonus of $60 per month for defects under 2%).
questions.model_answer: One drawback is weakened teamwork [k]. Paying $60 only for personal sub-2% months rewards individual effort over group success [app], so experienced blowers may stop helping juniors whose defect rates run closer to 4%, eroding the shared skills the workshop needs [an]. A second drawback is the temptation to hide defects [k]. Blowers chasing $60 could pass flawed tubes on to the 14 packers for shipment [app], and faulty laboratory tubing reaching hospitals would mean returns, lost contracts and a damaged reputation far costlier than the bonus pool [an].

knowledge_max_2: Individual rewards can undermine teamwork / helping colleagues
Individual rewards can encourage hiding defects / cutting corners
application_max_2: Reference to $60 per month / sub-2% defect target / juniors near 4%
Reference to 14 packers / laboratory tubing reaching hospitals
analysis_max_2: Chain from individual reward to rivalry to lost shared learning / rising 4% rate

questions.question_text: Do you think Clearway Glassworks should choose Option A? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A is straightforward and equal: 3% of annual profit, about $70,000 this year, split equally among all 66 staff, gives blowers and packers the same stake [k]. On Herzberg's view, financial reward is a hygiene factor — a profit share will not by itself create lasting drive — but it signals the firm values everyone and costs nothing until profits exist [app]. Equal sharing, however, links blower effort only weakly to the payout: each of the 66 staff receives roughly $1,060 whether or not their own defects fell [an]. Option B ties $60 per qualifying month directly to quality: under 2% defects, up to 5 months a year, worth $300 extra for top blowers [k]. It attacks the actual 4% defect rate with a clear personal target and leaves the $1,380 salary untouched [app]. But it ignores the packers entirely, may breed rivalry among the 52 blowers, and does not address why quit rates hit 15% a year [an]. Overall, I think Clearway should choose Option A first, then layer Option B on next year [eval] because equal profit sharing builds firm-wide loyalty at predictable cost, while the individual bonus can be added once defect data is reliable [eval].

scenario_stem:
Marlin Rope & Twine Factory is a private limited company in Country X producing marine rope from synthetic fibre. It employs 44 spinners, 16 finishers and 6 office staff. Annual output is 820,000 metres of rope and revenue is $3.1 million. Spinners are paid $9.80 per hour. Over the past 2 years, absenteeism has reached 11% and 3 experienced spinners retired, leaving skill gaps.

The director, Calum Reyes, is deciding how to motivate the shop floor before a 9-month export contract worth $540,000. Option A: job rotation so spinners alternate between spinning and finishing every 3 months. Option B: appoint 4 team leaders from the spinners at $280 per month extra, giving responsibility for quality checks and training new starters. He must choose by the end of the month.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'profit sharing'.
questions.model_answer: Profit sharing is a financial reward in which a portion of the business's profit is paid out to employees, usually as a bonus, so staff benefit when the company succeeds and lose when it does not [2].

knowledge_max_2: A portion of the business's profit is paid to employees
Usually paid as a bonus; reward depends on company success

questions.question_text: Explain two non-financial methods Marlin Rope & Twine could use to motivate its spinners.
questions.model_answer: One non-financial method is job rotation [k]. Alternating spinners between spinning and finishing every 3 months varies the routine and cuts boredom behind the 11% absenteeism rate across 820,000 metres of annual output [app]. A second non-financial method is giving responsibility through team leaders [k]. Appointing 4 spinners at $280 per month extra to lead quality checks and train new starters would satisfy Herzberg's responsibility motivator and plug the skill gaps left by 3 experienced spinners retired recently [app].

Responsibility / team leadership is a Herzberg motivator

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of Option B (appointing 4 team leaders at $280 per month extra).
questions.model_answer: One advantage is faster transfer of skills [k]. Four experienced spinners can coach new starters on quality while spinning and finishing continue as normal [app], preserving craft knowledge lost when 3 experienced spinners retired and protecting the $540,000 export contract [an]. A second advantage is stronger motivation of the leaders themselves [k]. The role brings recognition and responsibility — Herzberg's key motivators — beyond money [app], which should lift effort and morale across the 44 spinners as quality checks are enforced consistently each shift [an].

knowledge_max_2: Experienced staff coach/train newcomers / transfer skills
Responsibility and recognition are Herzberg motivators

Reference to $540,000 export contract / 44 spinners

questions.question_text: Do you think Marlin Rope & Twine should choose Option B? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option B creates 4 team-leader roles at $280 per month extra — about $1,120 per month, small against $540,000 of export revenue and $3.1 million annual output [k]. Responsibility and recognition are Herzberg motivators, so the chosen leaders should work harder and lift the 44 spinners around them through quality checks and onboarding of new starters [app]. This directly targets the skill gaps from 3 retirements and the 11% absenteeism problem before the 9-month export contract begins [an]. Option A, by contrast, spreads skills wider [k]. Job rotation between spinning and finishing every 3 months builds flexibility so anyone can cover either role, though it does nothing about pay, leadership or the loss of specialist mentors [app]. Rotation is free to implement and affects all 44 spinners equally, whereas only 4 get the extra responsibility [an]. Overall, I think Option B is the better choice [eval] because the urgent issue is skill loss and quality leadership on a $540,000 contract — 4 motivated team leaders fix that now, while rotation can be added later [eval].

scenario_stem:
Redbank Paper Mill is a public limited company producing corrugated cardboard in Country X. The mill employs 118 workers across 3 shifts and pays $10.10 per hour. Output is 1.4 million square metres per quarter, and fibre waste reached 8.5% of raw material last quarter. Fibre recycling trials recovered a further 3% last quarter. The operations director, Tomas Lindqvist, wants to cut waste before the annual shareholders' meeting in June.

He is considering two approaches. Option A: a job enrichment programme letting line teams decide on quality checks and stop the line when defects appear, plus a weekly feedback board. Option B: an across-the-board pay rise of 5% to $10.61 per hour for all 118 workers, on the argument that better-paid staff work with more care. Costings are due in 3 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'hygiene factors'.
questions.model_answer: In Herzberg's two-factor theory, hygiene factors are job-related conditions such as pay, working conditions, company policy and supervision; if they are inadequate they cause dissatisfaction, but improving them does not by itself create motivation [2].

knowledge_max_2: Conditions such as pay / working conditions / policy / supervision
Their absence causes dissatisfaction; improving them does not by itself motivate

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using pay alone to motivate workers at Redbank Paper Mill.
questions.model_answer: One limitation is that pay is a hygiene factor [k]. Raising wages to $10.61 per hour stops dissatisfaction but soon becomes the expected norm, so the extra motivation fades after the first few pay packets [app]. A second limitation is that pay does not change behaviour at the machine [k]. Workers can be paid 5% more yet still watch waste run at 8.5% of raw material, because money adds no authority to stop the line or set quality checks [app].

knowledge_max_2: Pay is a hygiene factor — becomes expected norm / effect fades
Money alone does not give authority to change working methods
application_max_2: Reference to $10.61 per hour / 5% pay rise / $10.10 per hour
Reference to 8.5% fibre waste / all 118 workers

questions.question_text: Explain two arguments in favour of Option A (the job enrichment programme).
questions.model_answer: One argument is responsibility and ownership [k]. Letting line teams decide on quality checks and stop the line meets Herzberg's responsibility motivator and gives crews real authority over defects [app], so problems are fixed at source and the 8.5% fibre waste figure should fall sharply [an]. A second argument is shared visibility of results [k]. A weekly feedback board shows waste and output figures to all 118 workers, turning improvement into a shared challenge [app], and shared visibility plus ownership should cut waste per 1.4 million square metres produced each quarter [an].

knowledge_max_2: Job enrichment adds responsibility / authority over work
Feedback/visibility of results motivates improvement
application_max_2: Reference to line teams deciding on quality checks / stop the line
Reference to weekly feedback board / 118 workers / 8.5% fibre waste

Chain from visible figures to shared challenge to lower waste per quarter

questions.question_text: Do you think Redbank Paper Mill should choose Option A? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A gives teams the authority and the information to act [k]. Stop-the-line power and a weekly feedback board target the actual problem — 8.5% fibre waste — and add Herzberg motivators such as responsibility, achievement and recognition rather than a one-off wage bump [app]. Cutting waste by even a couple of percentage points across 1.4 million square metres per quarter would save far more than a 5% pay rise costs [an]. Option B is simpler and universal [k]. A 5% rise to $10.61 per hour rewards all 118 workers equally, is easily understood and looks decisive before the June shareholders' meeting [app]. However, Herzberg warns pay is only a hygiene factor, so workers may welcome $10.61 briefly then coast, and the higher wage bill is permanent with no guaranteed fall in waste [an]. Overall, I think Option A is the better choice [eval] because the mill's central problem is waste, not pay — enrichment fixes it at source and builds a quality culture within the 3 weeks available [eval].

Job enrichment = stop-the-line authority / feedback / responsibility

scenario_stem:
Westbrook Industrial Coatings is a private limited company painting steel tanks and beams in Country X. It employs 58 spray-painters and 8 QA inspectors across 2 lines. Annual revenue is $5.6 million and rejections average 6%. Rejections cost an estimated $340,000 last year. Painters are paid $11.90 per hour. Managing Director Grace Ellison sees 20% staff turnover in the painting booths and wants to improve motivation before quoting for a 3-year infrastructure contract.

She is weighing two options. Option A: a share-ownership scheme granting paint-shop staff shares worth up to $4,000 each after 2 years' service. Option B: a job-enrichment programme letting 10 coach painters lead daily briefings and approve first-off checks, plus $75 monthly recognition bonuses. Grace must decide in 4 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'share ownership'.
questions.model_answer: Share ownership is a financial reward in which employees are given or can buy shares in the company, making them part-owners who gain when the business is profitable and its shares rise in value [2].

knowledge_max_2: Employees are given or can buy shares in the company
They become part-owners / gain from profit and rising share value

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the 20% staff turnover in the painting booths should concern Westbrook Industrial Coatings.
questions.model_answer: One reason is replacement cost [k]. Recruiting and training a spray-painter is expensive, and constant turnover means juniors keep leaving before mastering the spray technique [app]. A second reason is rising rejections [k]. New painters make more mistakes, so the 6% rejection rate and the $340,000 it cost last year could climb further as 20% of the 58 spray-painters are replaced [app].

Inexperienced staff make more mistakes / quality falls
application_max_2: Reference to 20% turnover / 58 spray-painters
Reference to 6% rejections / $340,000 cost last year

questions.question_text: Explain two strengths of Option B (the job-enrichment programme).
questions.model_answer: One strength is immediate motivation through responsibility [k]. Ten coach painters lead daily briefings and approve first-off checks — Herzberg's responsibility and recognition motivators in action [app], and coach-led checks catch spray faults early, helping to cut the 6% rejection rate on tanks and beams [an]. A second strength is visible, targeted recognition [k]. The $75 monthly recognition bonuses reward genuine achievement without raising everyone's pay bill — ten coaches at $75 is only $750 per month [app], while daily briefings spread best practice to new painters far faster [an].

knowledge_max_2: Responsibility and recognition are Herzberg motivators
Targeted bonuses reward achievement without universal pay rise
application_max_2: Reference to 10 coach painters / daily briefings / first-off checks / $75 per month
Reference to 6% rejection rate / tanks and beams

Chain from daily briefings to faster skill spread to protected quality and lower turnover

questions.question_text: Do you think Westbrook Industrial Coatings should choose Option A? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A offers a $4,000 shareholding after 2 years' service — a long-term stake aligning paint-shop staff with company success on a possible 3-year infrastructure contract [k]. Shares make employees part-owners with a reason to protect quality, echoing Maslow's esteem needs and Herzberg's recognition of achievement [app]. But 2 years is a long wait to change behaviour now, the 20% turnover may not improve before the quote in 4 weeks, and share value depends on the $5.6 million revenue holding up [an]. Option B applies Herzberg's motivators — responsibility and recognition — straight away [k]. Ten coach painters lead daily briefings and approve first-off checks, and $75 monthly recognition bonuses reward the 10 coaches directly, costing just $750 per month [app]. It directly attacks the 6% rejection rate and 20% turnover before the infrastructure quote is signed, and can be running inside the 4 weeks available [an]. Overall, I think Option B is the better first step [eval] because responsibility and recognition fix the booth problems immediately, while share ownership's 2-year vesting is too slow to cut 20% turnover before the quote [eval].

Herzberg: responsibility and recognition are motivators acting quickly
